title: why the mind talks to itself
subtitle: what inner speech is for, and why "you" helps

steps.text: most people have a voice that narrates, plans and comments. it's one of the mind's everyday tools.
children start by talking out loud to themselves while they play or work something out. with time, that talk goes quiet and moves inside.
researchers think inner speech helps with planning, remembering and sticking with a task. how much people use it varies a lot from person to person.
steps.evidence: moderate (a review of many studies; inner speech is hard to measure)

steps.text: when does the inner voice get busiest?

options.label: when i'm planning
options.reply: that fits. planning is one of the jobs it seems to do well.

options.label: when something's on the line
options.reply: that's common. the voice gets loud when things matter.

options.label: when it's quiet and i'm alone
options.reply: that makes sense. with fewer distractions, it has room to talk.

steps.text: so the voice is useful. the grammar it uses matters a little too. "i" keeps us close to the feeling. a name steps back a bit.

steps.prompt: try the same thought two ways:
lines: {name}'s nervous about tomorrow, and that makes sense.
steps.reply: neither is the right one. the second one just adds some distance, the way a friend has.

steps.text: in seven studies, people who used "you" or their own name before a stressful task tended to feel less threatened by it, and dwelled on it less afterward.

steps.prompt: when might a step back be useful? pick any:
options: before a conversation i'm looking forward to
steps.reply: good ones. nothing to do about them right now. just worth knowing.

steps.prompt: write a line to borrow, using a name:
ideas: can take this one step at a time.

steps.text: inner speech is a tool, and a small change in grammar, a name instead of "i", can give the distance a friend has.
once today, when your mind comments on something, say one sentence of it with your name instead of "i".

grounding.idea: inner speech develops from talking aloud in childhood, and supports planning and self-regulation
self-talk using "you" or one's name reduced anxiety and rumination under stress
